analysis.title: "Seven Times Higher": Goldman Dissects The $20 Tanker Premium, And Finds 4 Of 5 Drivers Won't Go Away While The War Lasts
key_insights: Goldman's 25-route freight index shows the global average crude freight rate rose from about $3/bbl a year ago to above $20/bbl. Middle Eastern routes are above $35/bbl. The rate is seven times higher than a year ago.

Goldman splits the $20/bbl year-over-year rise (14-day average) into five drivers: Hormuz war risk premium $7/bbl, ship-to-ship transfers $4/bbl, maritime fuel costs $4/bbl, inefficient tanker allocation and redirections $3/bbl, and the US blockade of Iran's fleet $2/bbl.
Goldman expects four of the five drivers to persist while the Middle East conflict lasts. It treats the recent dip in freight rates as an easing risk premium, not a fix to the underlying logistics.

The Hormuz premium is measured by comparing Murban at Fujairah (east of the Strait) with Basrah (west of it). That premium is up $35/bbl year over year to over $40. About one sixth of global seaborne crude transits Hormuz, which converts to $7/bbl on the global freight average.

About one sixth of tankers in the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman do ship-to-ship transfers on any given day. Kpler data shows a Gulf of Oman VLCC doing STS work takes 23 days round trip versus 10 for a direct Hormuz run.
Global marine fuel prices are up nearly $50/bbl, or 70%. Weak bunker exports from the Gulf and Russia meet steady demand from tankers and container ships.

Half of available VLCCs are sailing in ballast, 4 percentage points more than a year ago. Smaller ships are pushed onto long-haul routes, and Red Sea and Black Sea detours add to the $3/bbl allocation cost.

Iran's fleet on the water is down nearly 40% year over year, with most loaded ships used as floating storage. Iranian oil and tankers used to cover 1.7mb/d of Asian crude demand, and those buyers now compete for non-sanctioned ships.

Goldman's baseline has Brent falling to $90/bbl by year-end and averaging $80/bbl in 2027. Even so, continued ship-to-ship transfers would be needed without reliable freedom of navigation through Hormuz. The US blockade is unlikely to be lifted without a peace deal.
Goldman lists higher freight rates for longer as an upside risk to its Brent forecast.

US plans to let sanctioned dark fleet tankers go through a process to ship legitimately are seen as marginal relief by Goldman's commodities desk (Thomas Evans). Goldman's framework puts this at the $2 Iran-fleet component at most.

Because crude benchmarks are priced free-on-board, high freight forces distant producers to discount. Middle Eastern producers ship nearly half their crude long-haul and are discounting heavily, especially Gulf-loaded grades (Basrah, Upper Zakum, Al Shaheen).

The Brent-WTI spread widened to $14/bbl last week versus a usual $5 as US producers cut prices to keep nearly 2mb/d flowing to Europe. US Gulf crude arrivals in Europe fell to about 1.64mb/d in October from 1.89mb/d in September.
Crude close to its buyers benefits. North Sea Brent strengthened in the first half of October on European and Mediterranean demand, and Russia's ESPO picked up some Asian demand.
The spread then narrowed. TD25 came off $8/bbl from its highs and WTI/Brent rallied about $4.5. On Tuesday's settles, December Brent was $108.79 and expiring November WTI was $101.79.

Chinese and other Asian refiners import 50% and 80% of crude via long-haul routes, so freight is a larger share of their feedstock cost. Goldman says Asian refining margins are likely approaching levels where further freight increases would be hard to absorb.

Gross refining margins remain very high, but net margins fell over the last month on higher transport, energy and regulatory costs. European refiners cut crude imports and runs over the last two weeks.
Goldman says lower net margins could raise global refined product prices. High freight widens crude differentials, supports product prices and suppresses refiners' net margins.

ZeroHedge's read: at least $13 of the $20 freight bill (Hormuz toll, shuttle and Iran blockade) comes directly from the war. Falling freight reflects the risk premium easing and refiners' reduced willingness to pay, not relief.

sector_views.rationale: High freight and operating costs are pushing net refining margins lower even as gross margins stay high. European refiners are cutting runs and Asian margins are near levels where more freight cost is hard to absorb.
Freight rates are up sevenfold year over year but have edged down in recent days as the risk premium eased. Goldman expects most drivers to persist while the conflict lasts.
High Gulf Coast-to-Europe freight pushed the Brent-WTI spread to $14/bbl, forcing US producers to cut prices to keep exports flowing.

tension_points.bull_case: Global freight rates have edged down over recent days, which could read as easing in shipping costs.
tension_points.bear_case: Goldman attributes the dip to an easing risk premium and refiners' reduced willingness to pay, not fixed logistics. Four of five drivers, at least $13 of the $20, are tied to the war and persist without a peace deal.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A peace deal that restores freedom of navigation through Hormuz and lifts the US blockade of Iran's fleet.

theme_stances.key_argument: Four of five freight drivers are tied to the war and will keep freight elevated while the conflict lasts.
theme_stances.evidence: likely continue to support global freight rates as long as the conflict on the Middle East persists

theme_stances.key_argument: High freight lowers refiners' net margins, cuts runs and could raise refined product prices.
theme_stances.evidence: could raise global refined product prices
